I just picked Orwell up in the sale, thought it looked interesting. It was. VERY. 
The game's premise is a controversial one, and one that could merit debate for hours, and it explores this concept well, on multiple situations. The morality of what you, and ultimately the people you're working against do is questioned numerous times. 

If however, you're not looking at a question of ethics, I'd still reccomend this game, although a tad on the short side (I completed it in under 6 hours), the story and game content is fun and gets you really thinking. Having to filter information and disregarding things said out of context instead of just dragging and dropping everything in was a nice touch. The gameplay is solid, the visuals are ok, the music is good and builds atmosphere. All in all, a good game.

I only hope that they add more cases, even as a DLC, otherwise once you have played through the game once, the gripping story would certainly lose its charm.

TL:DR - Good solid game, limited replayability, short completion time. Hoping for more content. Worth £5 from the sale.

A short game about a Dystopian present where everything you say online can be used against you.

Most of it is viewed through the lens of the the Orwell software; allowing you to read through calls, emails, news reports and webpages searching for data to build up profiles for the authorities to use. The only face who even knows of your existence can only talk to you through a one-way communicator and only see the data you post back but the lives you explore are far from being flat characters.

The game was released as an episodic one (all the parts are now out) with each episode being a day. The writing on each gives some huge hooks and cliffhangers which will make you want to keep going and get to the bottom of the situation. The accompanying art-style really makes this game stand out for me, and I would heartily recommend this game, especially to anybody who has an itch to scratch until "Need to know" comes out.

If you like games with a lot of actual gameplay this isn't for you. But if you like story-driven, psychological thrillers that keep you guessing, you're in for a treat. 

The UI and art style is extremely crisp and surprisingly uncluttered considering the amount of stuff you constantly have to click through. Articles and conversations are well-written, and the characters have a lot of personality.

The music/sound is minimal, but the game does a great job of using it to increase drama during major discoveries.

Story is really good, by far the highlight of the game. Without spoiling anything, there are lots of twists that you don't really see coming. And I have to say, the game manages to get a lot of emotion into a game with no voice acting. You really do start to feel for some of these characters at times. 

Overall, if you really like this type of game it will be worth $10. It is short (I've beaten it in about 4.5 hours) but it never feels like it's dragging on to the point where I just wish it would end. It's just solid action from start to finish. One of my favorite games of 2016.

Orwell is a game that has motivated me to take the time to write a review again, something I have not done in a while.  I'll admit, the title using the name of the author of a favorite book of mine grabbed my attention, and the description of the gameplay was enough to get me to take the plunge during the winter sale.  What followed was several hours spent parsing through the personal data of a group of fictional persons to solve the mystery of a terror attack and to consider the tradeoffs between privacy and security.

Let me start by saying that Orwell is at no point pedantic.  On the very rare occassion a character has been preachy, it was entirley in character for an activist.  This game has you violating privacy in order to achieve a verifiable and practical good; if you are a successful investigator you can literally save lives.  I'd do a diservice to potential players though to say any more than the very vague and cliche question of "At what cost?"

The gameplay is surprisingly interesting and reminded me is a lot of ways of the surprise hit "Papers, Please."  In the not-to-distant future The Party has enacted a new security measure that gathers every scrap of digital information a person could leave.  However, to address internal privacy concerns no one person sees everything and makes decisions.  You play an "Investigator" who has been hired to comb through relevant data as determined by the search algorythims of the Orwell system.  As you read people's emails, chatlogs, and visit their blogs and social media sites you decide what information to pass onto your Advisor.  His role is to determine who merits investigation and draw conclusions from the data you send.  That is to say, the only information the insider in law enforcement is allowed to see is what you deem relevant.  To do your job well you must avoid not only missing relevant data, but oversharing data that could be taken out of context or is irrelevant.  Of course, since it is completley up to you to decide what is relevant, this opens the door to different investigation outcomes I fully intend to explore in future playthroughs, even if I do know the answer to the mystery.

The mystery is also quite enthralling.  I write this review at 3AM, having completed the game in a single sitting of several hours, sucked in by the need to uncover "just one more" piece of the puzzle until suddenly I was furiously not only trying to solve the whole riddle, but making ethical considerations over what I should share or if I should continue to do my job "properly."  If you enjoy a good mystery or if you like very interactive VN-style games like Analogue: A Hate Story (which I also reccomend), then I can't tell you to buy this quickly enough, even if it isn't on sale.  This was a unique and wonderful gaming experience that I am glad I had.

This game made me question my moral compass several times, is surveillance bad? I mean it reduces crime rates, was thought bad? Were the people in thought actively trying to harm people? Is what I'm doing bad? Another thing I loved was the soundtrack. The way the music got more intense when some big thing came up it really put you on your toes. The plot twists were fantastic also. And I loved the gameplay, it was reminissant of papers please, a game I and many others loved, and the idea for the gameplay was executed so well it was fun, it didn't get boring reading as you were uncovering a mystery the entire way which kept you intrigued. The fact I can play in multiple ways, either I can read deep into everything or I can just simply skim, I loved it. The game messed with my emotions, even making me stressed at times because I had absolutely no idea what to do in the situation and my decision would drastically change the gameand I actually felt bad when I made the wrong decision, no game has ever really done that. At first comment, this is much more a novel / interactive story than a game.

I really enjoyed it. It's a narative focused game about struggling to find the roots of a series of terrorist attacks in the city. I was really impressed by the nuance to it, there is no comically evil villain. Each character feels believable with real emotion, and behaves like a human being, to the point that you do start to have second thoughts about your mission and your motives in a very organic, real way. For a game that I assumed was giong to have a message about surveillance, it wasn't nearly as heavy handed as I expected and was a genuinely interesting, intriguing ride through. Even knowing who the suspects are, it manages to keep you guessing not just about the attacks, but the people everybody involved in the game. It may be short, but there's some replayability and I think its easily worth the 10USD.  Also the soundtrack is gnarly af.

one of the few games where your choices truly influence the course of the story. Orwell is a well crafted story driven game with a strong theme and well thought out story. Replayability is high. The story choices you can make encourage the player to complete several playthroughs in order to discover the other outcomes. I Highly reccommend this game to anyone who likes story above action, or to anyone who is looking for a different experience.

The layout of the game is simple to understand and the tutorial doesn't treat you as if you're an absolute noob. The story is complex - so complex that every choice you make is connected to other choices and so on until an ending is reached. There are three endings (that I've found), but each end result is different depending on your choices. 
Believe me when i say that this game will keep you guessing so much that you'll want to play it over and over simply to see all the options. Prepare yourself for an amazing soundtrack too - the music combines perfectly with each event in the game and gets more and more intense with every episode (something that - as a music lover - i fell in love with immeadiatly).
You might find you're heart jumping when you discover another clue, due to the highs and lows of the soundtrack. this game will have you thinking like a detective and acting like a savior - or like an enemy. Sympathetic or apathetic to the characters at hand - it's garanteed that you'll enjoy peering into the lives of these complicated people!

Long story short: I would recommend this game. That being said, I had a lot of criticisms--so forgive me if the rest of this seems self-contradictory. There are plenty of other reviews that thoroughly cover what the game does well. 

After the intriguing trailer, I found the first two episodes dissappointing. The art style was clean and pleasant as expected, but I found the characters to be boring and slightly unlikable, which prevented much investment in the story. 

However, the game does shift as you progress through later episodes--interesting developments, twists, overturned expectations. It wasn't phenomenal, but I did get invested, and found the whole experience ultimately worth purchasing.

My biggest problem with the game--some of it felt like a trudge through data files, rather than the investigative puzzle I hoped for. The few times I was prompted with a high stakes question, where my answer actually mattered, I felt like I had to find the answer through mindless clicking, rather than any logic or puzzle solving. It felt a little pointless, honestly.

In sum, I felt like the game didn't quite live up to its potential--although there were definitely moments where I felt for the characters, and was confronted with the discomfort and ethical ambiguity of violating their privacy. I was put in tense situations, was surprised, and had some control over the course of events. Despite my disappointment in the beginning, I really enjoyed the final episodes. So that's why I would recommend this game--Orwell has a novel premise that was executed fairly well, and it's defintiely an experience worth having.

Before I bought this game, I was really wondering whether I was just stuffing more money down the drain. Turns out I wasn't. I could say this was the most constructive and thoughtful four hours I have spent completing a game on Steam.

This is one of the few games which make you think. How could Orwell work in a real life environment? What if Orwell was inspected by a unbiased individual? As you can see, the game has also managed to create a direct link to security forces in real life. They spark thoughts and theories about how Orwell could work or not; and whether the public (in said real life) would approve of the system.

Theories aside, let me move on to my pros and cons before I bore all of you scrollers:
[i]Pros[/i]
[list]
   [*]Very dynamic storyline, with multiple possible endings and sub-endings
   [*]The game makes you regret doing things which you're not meant to do, such as ignoring datachunks, especially when it's about not letting a suspect escape [spoiler]except for initiate's pug profile pic, that's an exception[/spoiler]
   [*]Keeps the game interesting at all times; there is no drop of tension except for the end of a chapter
[/list]

[i]Cons[/i] ; some spoilers ahead!
[list]
   [*]The story ended a bit too early for my liking; [spoiler] I would have liked to research more about Thought and initiate (Themba) to really clear up gaps of knowledge [/spoiler]
   [*]There could have been a cinematic at the end, just like there was in the beginning - [spoiler] instead of four zoomed in TNB articles. [/spoiler]
   [*]Unable to do anything in the epilogue of the game if you click anywhere except for what you're supposed to do.
[/list]

All in all, a great game. If you're in the process of thinking "will I regret it?", rest assured that all you will possibly regret is having finished the game too quickly.

I shall have to come back and edit this review after more playing/when I'm not sleep deprived but right now I just felt the need to post my first ever Steam review because this game has really grabbed me like nothing else.

Downloaded Orwell on a whim about 4 hours ago, opened it and thought I'd have a look whilst I readied myself for bed. Four hours later, I'm lying here in the same position clutching my laptop, heart racing from endless twists and turns and from surprisingly genuine moments of fear. 

Story and characters are well done - I found myself having biases towards/against certain characters and so was very shocked when things didn't work out as I'd expected. The way the player is brought into the game towards the end is also excellent - you feel like your choices matter and as if you are actually under threat. Details of characters' lives were interesting to explore, and I thought the conversation felt pretty real (unlike in many other games where transcripts of conversation are robotic and plainly fake). The game may be based around looking for bits of evidence in conversation/documents a la 'Papers, Please' but this is infinitely more gripping with none of the drab routine that I sometimes find a little tiring in PP. 

Of course, as a bit of a George Orwell fan, I was probably predisposed to enjoy this - and there are many 1984 references scattered throughout which will be provide amusement for fans of his work. The design/interface is very pleasant - very modern but not overly so in a way that makes it sci-fi; one of the scary things about 'Orwell' is how realistic this dystopia really is. If you care to let it be, this game is a very interesting and thought-provoking way to consider the ethics of state surveillance. I happen to have gone into playing with a very strong opinion on the issue but I think the game is well balanced in the way it allows you to hold any perspective/develop your own opinion (the narrative in the game is such that you could argue both for and against the government-snooper employment of the player). 

Concerns/negatives: I worry that the game is very short - I reached an end after my four hours of feverish play. There would appear to be other endings I can explore so I eagerly look forward to doing that after some sleep, but I don't know how much more there is for me to discover and I guess I'll have to edit this after a bit more exploring. I've achieved a half of the achievementh so there's evidently more to do, but this still is definitely not a game which goes on and on forever (shame - I really didn't want it to end). 



* All of this is written at 5am when I'm rather sleep-deprived after racing through the game so apologies for lack of clarity/usefulness. Tl;dr I really enjoyed this so much. Even if after further exploration I realise there isn't much more to the game, I'm still definitely not sad I parted with ~£7 for this. Would definitely recommend

Orwell lets you datamine in order to stop a terrorist plot, but not all is as it seems. What will your role be in the future of The Nation?
Using very unique mechanics Orwell tasks the player with only one goal: Upload all information needed to solve the ongoing terrorist investigation. It is now up to you to decide what that means.
Engrossing and interesting story that had me weighing every choice carefully.

***MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD***

This game serves as a curious, yet chilling, simulation of what may happen to society as our technology, and deep desire for safety, continue to evolve.  

It starts off simple enough: there's basically been a terrorist attack, and you are the son-of-a-gun assigned to sort through tons of data from all kinds of digital sources, including the internet, emails, and even phone calls, to profile and ultimately make decisions on, people and situations that have far-reaching effects on darn near everything.

This game is not for everyone, as it requires attention to detail, and a keen yet curious mind. Naturally, many will get bored or disappointed quickly, as the game isn't about action but rather the intellectual journey. The sound effects at key moments were a nice touch too.

The theme of the game is very interesting, particulary if you enjoyed 1984 book or like conspiracy theories. Beside that I cannot recomend the game mostly because I find it very simplish for it`s price... it`s just a point and click on web pages, some kind of modern read tale where you  can make choices by selecting bunch of data from websites.

Overall, this little story based game was really intriguing, and it really felt like you were the investigator looking for clues as to what is going on in the Nation

In [i]Orwell[/i], you are an investigator, employed by a nondescript democratic nation to dig through news, intercepted communications, websites, and personal computers in order to unravel a mystery.

It's not a simulation so much as an interactive story, with several routes to the end, and several possible fates for many of the characters.

Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terrorist attacks. Your job is solely to go through a heap of modern-day data, everything from standard phone numbers, police files and bank account details, through to more dubious emails, blogs and social media posts. Collecting information, looking for clues, flagging any possible suspects and chasing them down.

You can decide how much of the information you want to sift through as the data chunks are highlighted in blue and easily stand out. There are five episodes in total with each one structured as a ‘day’ and the gameplay will be on average one hour per episode.

A lot of effort went into creating the content for [i]Orwell[/i] and it is really impressive. It’s simple but fun with unexpected twists along the way. Orwell is an excellent experience.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Fascinating Story
- Convincing characters and plot
- Impactful choices and discoveries
- Complex and Innovative
- Fitting soundtrack

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Text logs of phone conversations feel unnatural

TL;DR: great game buggered by stupid save system. 

Orwell is a great game, no two ways about it. Easy to get into, nice story and so forth. I didn't have a problem with any of those things, however why have I then thumbed it down? 

Simple, this game, like so many others nowadays, have decided that the only save function this game needs is an autosave, meaning there is no way of backtracking, no way of re-doing things. One slip up and the game will laugh in your face and call you a tosser for the rest of the game, because that slip-up meant you didn't achieve what you wanted to do. I know some people are okay with that, they feel it's more immersive or whatever, but for me it is just a huge annoyance. "Realism" is all well and good, but they don't make the chat convos ingame take 5 minutes per post because while that'd be realistic, it's be annoying. For me it is the same thing here and it leaves me unable to really enjoy the game because it screws me over when I can't decide which of the two vague clues are the correct one. 

It is a crying shame, it's a great game but the save system isn't fun for me at all.

AN ACHIEVEMENTS REVIEW

-------------------------------------------------

Here's a review of the my experience while earning the achievements that you might find useful:

[b]It took me 3 full playthroughs to unlock 100% of the 27 achievements.[/b] At the moment, [spoiler]with some chapter(s) having 3 different endings - but most having 2[/spoiler], it is impossible to earn them all in any less than 3 playthroughs and you are guaranteed about 7 to 9 or so just by playing the 5 episodes in full once. [b]It took me 6 hours to complete the entire game[/b], genuinely following along and reading the content as a normal person would. The next playthrough was significantly less time at 4 hours, and even less on my last run: 2.5. Even if you aren't mindful of the achievements as you progress - say, you ended up missing a lot of optional things - you can still achieve 100% within 3 playthroughs in total; no worries.

My only gripe with this game is that after playing it once, your interest in the story drops considerably, and starting a new game can feel like "[i]going through the motions.[/i]" [spoiler]Even despite the changes in the story that occurs at the end of each episode due to your decisions, you can expect most of it will be the same across your 3 playthroughs, with the exception being a couple of episodes. I won't specify which, because that would spoil the experience...[/spoiler] Nonetheless, if you're patient in your first gameplay and take the time to remember a lot of things, you can easily speed through the last 2 runs. Alternatively, you may even choose to start 3 games simultaneously and finish them together (by completing an episode each, saving/quitting, and loading the next).

Games that carry heavy political overtones are hit or miss with me.  Orwell is one of those games that is a complete hit.  I had an idea of what to expect from the store page, but I had no idea that I was going to be glued to this game for 3 days straight.  The level of character development is amazing.  I think I went back and forth between hating and sympathizing with Harrison at least 5 times.  The story is the best part because you have control for the most part.  There are some things that you have to do for progression, but that is with any game.  A broad example so as not to spoil the game, you can make a person look completely innocent or incredibly guilty depending on what 'parts' of info you choose to share.  What parts of info will you provide to your adviser?  This game is well worth the asking price.  

Afterthought:  I don't know about anyone else, but I had a good LOL over the Queen of Bullshit part.

The UK citizens, can enjoy Orwell society in real life, as per Snooper's Charter. For everyone else, there is this game.

This game should become a part of a "Digital citizenship" curriculum for sure - there is no privacy on the internet and sometimes, there is no truth either. 

Orwell is, for sure, one of the few games concerning very recent and "hot" topics and does so perfectly. 
Although I suspected it would be anti-surveillance (it's called Orwell, after all), it positively surprised me. It did not push me at all not to cooperate with the government, it just let a few hints slip - like "We had to change the facts a bit to prevent panic" - sure, that's not a big deal, it's just the beginning, the first little white lie that ends in a dogma.

The best job Orwell does is making you feel helpless and powerfull all at once - only you know the whole story, you choose what Orwell knows and what it does not, you can set someone up or you can set them free but ultimately, you never know what the Agent is going to do...will he misinterpret the data and send someone to prison? Will he understand the reason you upload certain information? He never sees the "bigger picture", or the part of it that you have access to.
Are the people getting hurt really not on your conscience; did you JUST do your job? Are you really as impartial as you fancy yourself to be? What if it was your life being dissected?
I'm just filling space, but this game is great
